prompt.context: Our client is the health minister of a small country. The country is small and on the upper end of the GDP spectrum for countries of its size. The country's health system is completely free to its citizens and is funded by taxpayer money. Patients can visit one of 30 clinics spread throughout the country for a primary care visit, and then get referred to one of 2 larger hospitals if more intensive procedures are required. There are a few private systems for the richest citizens, but they are so small in comparison to the public system that they won't be considered. The GDP, and thus the tax returns for the country, have been growing at a 5% rate. However, the healthcare budget has required 10% growth to keep up with demand. The health minister is concerned that at this rate, the healthcare system will become unsustainable.
prompt.question: The health minister has hired us to figure out why the healthcare budget is requiring this level of growth and what can be done to reduce it.

clarifying_info.q: What is the current population of the country?
clarifying_info.a: The population is currently 1 million and the census estimates it will grow by 30% in 10 years.

exhibits.title: Census Bureau Population and Healthcare Cost Data
exhibits.shows: A table breaking down the population by age group (0-21, 22-65, 65+), showing the percentage of population today, the percentage of population in 10 years, and the average healthcare cost per person per year for each group.

framework: Demand-driven growth: demographic changes (aging population, population growth) leading to more visits
Demand-driven growth: changes in health perception/awareness causing citizens to seek care for issues previously ignored
Demand-driven growth: incentive systems of doctors/hospitals encouraging more visits or unnecessary referrals to the 2 hospitals
Supply-side effects: shortage of doctors or resources bidding up prices for the same services
Supply-side effects: lack of preventative care making patients less healthy and requiring more intensive care when ill

questions.prompt: What factors are driving the healthcare budget growth?
questions.guidance: Candidate should structure reasons into demand-side and supply-side drivers. Demand side: demographic aging, increased health awareness, perverse physician incentives (fee-for-service encouraging over-referral). Supply side: resource/doctor shortages raising costs, insufficient preventative care. A strong answer is MECE and covers both sides.

questions.prompt: What could the country do to cut costs, and what are the risks?
questions.guidance: Strong answers include: (1) Transparency — inform physicians of treatment costs so they factor cost into decisions; (2) Quotas/Rules — mandate generic drugs over branded, prefer outpatient procedures over inpatient stays; (3) Risk — rules must not compromise quality of care; physicians should be involved in crafting guidelines.

questions.prompt: Based on the census data, how much does the country currently spend on healthcare, and how much is it projected to spend in 10 years?
questions.guidance: Candidate should use the table to compute a population-weighted average cost per person, then multiply by total population now and in 10 years. Should note the shift in the 65+ cohort (doubling from 10% to 20%) as the main driver since that cohort costs 8x the 22-65 cohort. Should calculate the percentage increase unprompted or when pushed.

math.setup: Current spend = (population share × avg cost per person) × total population. Future spend = same formula with new shares and 1.3M population.
math.answer: Current spend: $950M; Projected spend in 10 years: $1.625B; approximately 71% increase.

questions.prompt: The health minister is considering a $5/visit copayment covering all individual visits. Currently the average citizen visits the healthcare system 5 times per year at an average cost of $50/visit. What would be the impact of the copayment on healthcare spending?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify two effects: (1) government cost per visit drops from $50 to $45 (patient pays $5); (2) visits per citizen may decline because visits are no longer free. After being told visits drop to 4.5/year, candidate should calculate new total cost and quantify the savings as a percent of the visit budget and as a percent of total spending.

math.setup: Current costs = visits/citizen × cost/visit × population. New costs = new visits/citizen × new cost/visit × population. Savings % of visit budget and of total budget.
steps: New cost per visit to government: $50 − $5 = $45
New visits per citizen per year: 4.5 (given)
math.answer: New visit costs: $202.5M, saving $47.5M (~19% reduction in visit spending, ~5% reduction in overall healthcare budget).

brainstorming.prompt: Although the copayment seems like a good idea, what are the risks associated with it? How could those risks be alleviated? Are there any other ideas aside from a copayment that could help?

categories.name: Equity / Affordability Risks
ideas: Poorest citizens may not be able to afford the $5 copay, reducing access to necessary care
Introduce a sliding scale copayment based on per capita income to protect low-income citizens

categories.name: Political / Public Acceptance Risks
ideas: The public will likely be unhappy with any charges for previously free care, creating political repercussions for the health minister
Conduct a survey to gauge public opinion before implementing; consider a phased rollout or communications campaign

categories.name: Deterrence Effectiveness Risks
ideas: $5 may not be enough to deter citizens who abuse the system with superfluous visits
Consider a sliding scale based on visit frequency or visit type to create stronger deterrence where needed

categories.name: Emergency Care Risks
ideas: The copayment could delay or discourage people from seeking emergency care
Waive the copayment for emergency situations

categories.name: Alternatives to Copayment
ideas: Limit certain visit types to a fixed frequency per year (e.g., eye exams once a year)
Increase investment in preventative care to reduce downstream illness and costly visits
Regulate or incentivize use of generic drugs over branded equivalents
Shift from inpatient stays to outpatient procedures where clinically appropriate

recommendation: Healthcare spending is projected to increase approximately 71% over the next 10 years, driven by both population growth (30%) and an aging demographic shift — the 65+ cohort will double from 10% to 20% of the population, and they cost 8× more per person than working-age adults.

A $5/visit copayment is a promising near-term lever that could reduce overall healthcare spending by roughly 5% (saving ~$47.5M), but it requires further analysis to confirm it will not reduce quality of care or create access inequities for low-income citizens.
risks: Copayment may disproportionately harm low-income citizens; a sliding income-based scale is needed
Public backlash and political risk must be managed carefully
Emergency care access must be protected (fee waiver for emergencies)
$5 deterrent effect may be insufficient for high-frequency abusers
next_steps: Conduct public survey to assess political feasibility of copayment
Design income-based sliding scale and emergency care exemptions
Evaluate visit-type regulations (e.g., annual caps on routine exams)
Develop a long-term preventative care program to reduce per-capita healthcare costs
Monitor and model the impact of aging demographics annually to adjust budget projections
